# Type: Strings {#sec-character}

{{< include ../preamble.qmd >}}


::: {style="margin-top: 1em; font-size: 125%; font-weight: 1000; text-align: center;"}
"Hello world!"
:::


The first exercice program is to be able to print a text on the console. This is in computer science. While this is trivial in programs like R, several concepts are need to that for programs in fortran, C, C++. And the tradition is to print "Hello world". The idea is somehow that you understand how a computer that you manage to prompt it to say hello to the world of the living.

A computer program is more than a basic calculator, it is should be obvious by now. A major difference or upgrade to computer program is that it can also handle non-number. And such object is called string and that's why printing "Hello world" string is lesson number 1.

Unlike number we cannot perform a arithmetic operation, you cannot multiply or divide letters or words. Manipulating them require non-mathematical operation although human natural: e.g. delete a letter or a word, combing text, replace text etc. For most of our purpose, we use string to represent qualitative variables. In other word, when you enter the data and have text "male" or "female", they are considered string--in contrast to numbers like height or weight.

## Formal {.unnumbered}
A string is a type of object, and is anything within quotation marks `""`
Each character is the encoded in a binary format 0 1. There are differnt types of encoding.

## Examples {.unnumbered}

```{r}
# It could be one letter
one_letter <- "R"

# It could be a word
a_word <- "Hello"

# It could be anything as long as it is within a quotation mark
long_string <- "Ny akoho tsy nanidina tsy nahandry ny andro zoma. Ny omby mahia tsy lelafin'ny namany..."
```

Here we create a string object called "sin"
```{r}
#| echo: true
"sin" # a text composed of three letters s
```

Here we create a variable named sin and store the character "sin"
```{r}
#| echo: true
sin <- "sin"
```


Using arithmetic operation on string throws an error because it is not defined

```r
string_1 <- "1" # is a character not a number
string_2 <- "2026" # is characters a not a number

string_1 + string_2
```

Combining strings with the function `paste()` and specify how they are separated by nothing `""`, by a comma, `","`, by comma and then space `", "`, or `" anything you want "`
```{r}
#| echo: true

paste("Hello", "world", sep = "")

paste("Hello", "world", sep = ",")

paste("Hello", "world", sep = ", ")

paste("Hello", "world", sep = " anything you want ")
```

Paste can take more words and used with variable instead of the value
```{r}
#| echo: true
paste("Hello", "world", "life", sep = " there ")

word1 <- "Hello"
word2 <- "world"

paste(word1, word2, word1, word2)
```


## Tips and warnings {.unnumbered}
- Semantic: string, character, factor.
- Unlike we can use any special character
```{r}
"There is problem in usin$ spécial, & < is not ! or 1 2 3"
```

- Manipulating strings requires special function that mostly related to pattern matching, subsitution/replace, deletion, insertion adding (using `paste()` above).
-  "Magadascar" is the sequence of letters and is different from "Madagascar". (As 12 is different from 21). While the latter is easy to separate, it is not easy to differentiate the former. Indeed typo is unavoidable. Errors and issues aries when one encode data for instance
- Lingering space: it is common to enter data in MS Excel or GUI like that. And not only we make typos (e.g. `"male"` and `"Male"`), a sneaky typo that will not show in excel is `"male "`. It is necessary to perform some data cleaning when importing data into R. More on the latter edition of this.
